answer: The submission is clear and honest but reads as a concept description rather than evidence-backed venture. Priority improvements: (1) Quantify the market with bottom-up math: households in the target neighborhood x share with a broken item per year x average ticket = serviceable revenue. Replace 'dozens of devices' and 'small percentage' with sourced figures, and add results from even a small primary-research effort (e.g., 50 resident surveys, landlord interviews, a pop-up weekend). (2) Show unit economics and a real break-even: give average ticket, parts margin, labor cost per repair, repair time, rent assumption, and a month-by-month first-year P&L with explicit assumptions. Eight to ten repairs per day is stated without derivation; demonstrate it is plausible given $10-$60 tickets and technician capacity. Track margins on current jobs and report them. (3) Present traction as evidence: document the landlord job (units, revenue, repeat potential), log all repairs completed, turnaround, customer satisfaction, and any testimonials or letters of intent from landlords and housing groups. 'First paying client' is promising but thin; convert it into proof of the B2B channel. (4) Validate demand and pricing: show willingness-to-pay data, especially for the $8 membership (how many members needed, expected churn, and whether it cannibalizes repair revenue). Consider whether to prioritize B2B contracts, which may offer steadier revenue than walk-in traffic. (5) Sharpen differentiation and defensibility: since barriers are weak, spell out concrete moats such as landlord contracts, membership lock-in, local reputation, recycling partnerships, and a documented diagnosis workflow, rather than relying on 'service quality.' (6) Address risks explicitly: liability and insurance for repairing electronics, warranty policy on repairs, parts sourcing and inventory risk, technician dependence on one person (Devon), right-to-repair and parts availability constraints, and seasonal student demand swings. (7) Make the funding ask precise: state the exact amount requested, an itemized use of funds (build-out, tools, inventory, runway), and what milestones it unlocks, plus a plan for the gap between prize money and the $40-50K need. (8) Strengthen the team section: identify the skill gaps (retail operations, lease negotiation, licensing, hiring) and name specific advisors or mentors, and address founders' post-graduation commitment and time availability. (9) Fix basic execution gaps: build a simple website or landing page, define customer acquisition channels with cost estimates (campus, landlords, community groups, social media), and add a clear timeline with measurable milestones. (10) Tighten the writing: lead with the traction and the ask, cut generic problem framing, add one or two concrete customer stories, and replace hedges like 'we believe' and 'still refining' with data or a stated plan to obtain it.
